abstract: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disorders, including a 25% chance of developing schizophrenia (SCZ). SCZ is prevalent in 0.4-0.7% of the population. Evidence suggests that the cognitive deficits of SCZ may be caused by neurodevelopmental disconnection due to impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) maturation and myelination. We hypothesized that the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome impairs OL life cycle progression, halting oligodendrocytes in their immature phase and preventing advancement to the mature stage. This in turn creates myelination changes, demonstrated by a decrease in myelin. To test this, we utilized a 22q11.2 deletion mouse model focusing on the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a late-myelinating brain region. We evaluated PFC regions (mPFC, dlPFC, mOFC, lOFC) in adolescent (P14 and P28) mutant mice and controls. Additionally, we examined the two-hit hypothesis of schizophrenia using a maternal separation model. At P28, mutant mice displayed a significant increase in immature OLs and mature OLs in the PFC, and a decrease in myelination and myelin process length compared to controls. At P14, mutant mice showed subtle reductions in oligodendrocyte precursor cells and subtle myelination alterations in the mPFC. When considering the two-hit hypothesis, we saw equivalent reductions in myelination in the genetic-only, environmental-only, and two-hit groups. Together, these data demonstrate that the 22q11.2 deletion impairs OL maturation and functional myelination between P14 to P28, a critical window for neurodevelopment. Examining the impact of SCZ on OLs could reveal key intervention targets before SCZ symptom onset, and may determine the role of OLs and the 22q11.2 deletion in neural disconnectivity in schizophrenia.
